ground_truth_core_content:
Introduction:
**1:** Both sections make the same core argument: single complex prompts feel intuitive but lead to unreliable, hard-to-debug systems, and the solution is breaking work into the four patterns this lesson covers. This version keeps a brief Lessons 1-4 recap but spends most of the section on the actual problem framing ("almost always leads to unreliable, hard-to-debug systems") rather than substituting the recap for the hook entirely, unlike three of the five other articles graded so far.

The Challenge with Complex Single LLM Calls:
**1:** Both sections cover the same core problems (debugging difficulty, inability to update one part without breaking others, lost-in-the-middle, accuracy decreasing with prompt complexity) and the same practical example end-to-end, including full FAQ/FAQList Pydantic classes.

The Power of Modularity: Why Chain LLM Calls?:
**1:** Both sections cover the same chaining definition and the same benefits (modularity, accuracy, debugging, flexibility) and downsides (latency, cost, information loss). The added assembly-line and "one genius vs. many specialists" analogies are additive - see depth/breadth_enhancement - and do not displace any expected idea.

Building a Sequential Workflow: FAQ Generation Pipeline:
**1:** Both sections cover the same 3-step chain, the same three functions and class names, combining them into sequential_workflow, and the same measured 22.20-second execution time.

Optimizing Sequential Workflows With Parallel Processing:
**1:** Both sections cover the same core moves: independent per-question work run concurrently, asyncio for I/O-bound operations, the same 8.98-second result, and the sequential-vs-parallel trade-off. The added aside about non-deterministic outputs and concurrency-management techniques is additive - see depth_enhancement.

Introducing Dynamic Behavior: Routing and Conditional Logic:
**0:** Both sections cover the need for routing, LLM-as-classifier, and divide-and-conquer (elaborated here with an explicit Business-Process-Management framing and cascading routing - see depth/breadth_enhancement). However, as in three of the five other articles graded, this section never mentions the billing-vs-technical-support example the expected section uses here specifically to preview Sections 6-7 - a missing substantive idea the guideline's own bullet list explicitly requests.

Building a Basic Routing Workflow:
**0:** Both sections cover classify_intent, the per-intent prompts, and handle_query with routing logic. However, as in every one of the six articles graded so far, the expected section's second worked example (the billing query) is dropped entirely, leaving only the technical-support example.

Orchestrator-Worker Pattern: Dynamic Task Decomposition:
**1:** Both sections cover the orchestrator decomposing the billing+return+status-update query into typed tasks, dispatching to workers, and a synthesizer combining results, with a final synthesized email matching the expected section's specific detail formats. The added master-worker/dynamic-query-decomposition analogies and the time-critical/information-loss limitation are additive - see depth/breadth_enhancement.

Conclusion:
**1:** Both sections recap the same four patterns and both preview future lessons. This version explicitly names both required forward references by lesson number - "tools (Lesson 6), perform complex reasoning (Lesson 7)" - matching the expected section's own lesson numbers exactly, and adds a further reference to a memory lesson beyond what the expected section covers. This is the most complete match on this specific point found across all six articles graded.
